name: Special Topics in Analytical Chemistry: Bioanalytical Chemistry
description: Lectures or conferences covering selected topics of current interest in analytical chemistry.

name: Analytical Chemistry Seminar
description: Attendance required of graduate majors in the analytical area. graduate course in analytical chemistry. Presentation of one seminar.

name: Advanced Principles of Organic Chemistry
description: Principles of organic chemistry and their application to reaction mechanisms.

name: Advanced Synthetic Organic Chemistry
description: Discussion and application of synthetic methodology.

name: Topics in Synthetic Organic Chemistry
description: Synthesis of complex organic molecules, with emphasis on recent developments in approaches and methods.

name: Organometallic Compounds
description: Properties of organometallic compounds, the nature of the carbon-metal bond, compounds of metals in groups 1, 2, 3, and 4, and transition metals.

name: The Chemistry of High Polymers
description: Fundamental polymer chemistry, with emphasis on the mechanisms of polymerization reactions and the relationship of physical properties to chemical constitution.

name: Enzyme Mechanisms
description: Principles of enzyme structure; isolation and purification; physical chemistry of enzyme/substrate interactions; general overview of classes; transition state theory and catalysis; types of chemical catalysis; survey of cofactors; example mechanisms; catalytic antibodies; ribozyme structure and catalysis.

name: Chemistry and Biology of Nucleic Acids
description: Principles of nucleic acid structure and function; protein/nucleic acid interactions with particular emphasis on transcriptional regulators and DNA and RNA polymerases; chemistry of phosphate hydrolysis and its application to enzyme mechanisms; evolution of novel RNA molecules capable of specific binding and catalysis.

name: Special Topics in Biological Chemistry Mechanisms: Antibiotics
description: Molecular evolution, bioinformatics and protein structure prediction, principles of molecular recognition, rational protein design, biotechnology, reengineered organisms, advanced biophysical techniques, and computational biology.

name: Special Topics in Organic Chemistry: CarbohydrateChem/Glycobiology
description: Chemistry of selected types of organic compounds, such as alkaloids, carbohydrates, natural products, steroids.

name: Organic Chemistry Seminar Presentation
description: Attendance required of graduate majors in the organic area. Presentation of one seminar.

name: Statistical Thermodynamics
description: Fundamental principles with applications to systems of chemical interest.

name: Chemical Bonding and Spectra I
description: Basic methods and applications of quantum chemistry; atomic structure; chemical bonding in diatomic and polyatomic molecules. Brief introduction to molecular spectroscopy.

name: Elements of Quantum Chemistry
description: Brief treatment of the Schrodinger equation, followed by a survey of applications to chemical problems.

name: Theory of Molecular Spectroscopy
description: Molecular energy levels, spectroscopic selection rules; rotational, vibrational, electronic, and magnetic resonance spectra of diatomic and polyatomic molecules.

name: Special Topics in Physical Chemistry: Artificial Intelligence
description: Lecture or conferences covering selected topics of current interest in physical chemistry.

name: Computational Chemistry
description: Software for computational chemistry; model building and molecular mechanics; molecular orbitals and electronic structure; optical, infrared, and magnetic resonance spectra; solvation effects and molecular dynamics; building large systems.

name: Physical Chemistry Seminar
description: Attendance required of graduate majors in physical chemistry. graduate course in physical chemistry. Presentation of one seminar.

name: Advanced Inorganic Chemistry I
description: Crystalline state; covalent bonding; acids, bases, and solvents, nonmetallic compounds of Groups II through VII with emphasis on structure and reactivity.

name: Advanced Inorganic Chemistry II
description: Electronic structure of metals and transition metal complexes; solution chemistry and reaction mechanisms at metal centers; redox reactions; introduction to organometallic and bioinorganic chemistry.

name: Applications of Physical Methods in Inorganic Chemistry
description: Principles and applications of spectroscopic methods to the solution of inorganic problems. Those techniques used most extensively in current inorganic research are treated.

name: Chemistry of Solid Materials
description: Structure and properties of solids; semiconductors and superconductors.

name: Inorganic Biochemistry
description: Role of elements in biology. Modern spectroscopic and physical methods for study of Group I and II metals, metalloenzymes, metal ion transport and storage, functions of nonmetals in biochemical systems, and biomedical/biotechnical applications of metals.

name: Special Topics in Inorganic Chemistry: X-Ray Crystallography
description: Lectures or conferences on selected topics of current research interest in inorganic chemistry.

name: Inorganic Chemistry Seminar
description: Attendance required of graduate majors in inorganic chemistry. graduate course in inorganic chemistry. Presentation of one seminar.

name: Chemical Dynamics
description: Basic concepts of rate laws, collision theory, and transition state theory; an introduction to reaction dynamics, structural dynamics, and quantitative structure-reactivity correlations.

name: Individual Problems, Advanced: INDIVIDUAL PROBS ADV
description: Double registration permitted. Assigned reading program or development of assigned experimental problem.

name: Supervised Research
description: Supervised Research

name: Advanced Topics in Chemistry: Responsible Conduct ofResearch
description: Discussion and evaluation of chemical research advances reported in current chemical literature. S/U

name: Chemistry Colloquium
description: Topics presented by visiting scientists and local staff members.

name: Internship in College Teaching
description: Required for Master of Science in Teaching students but available for students needing additional practice and direction in college-level teaching.

name: Research for Master's Thesis
description: Research for Master's Thesis

name: Special Topics in Theory of Atomic and Molecular Structure
description: Mathematical techniques used in atomic, molecular, and solid-state theory. The one-electron approximation and the general quantum-mechanical manybody problems. Selected advanced topics.

name: Advanced Research
description: Research for doctoral students before admission to candidacy. Designed for students with a master's degree in the field of study or for students who have been accepted for a doctoral program. Not appropriate for students who have been admitted to candidacy.

name: Research for Doctoral Dissertation
description: Research for Doctoral Dissertation

name: Radiochemistry
description: Radioactivity detection, radiochemical separations and analyses, radiochemistry laboratory techniques, the practice of radiological safety, and tracer applications of radioisotopes in chemistry and other fields.

name: Translation Method: Chinese to English
description: Hands-on introduction to the processes, procedures, and cultural and linguistic challenges relevant to translation from Chinese to English. Development of basic translation skills including strategies on word level, sentence level, and text level. Acquisition of lexicon, structure, and style used in various fields (legal, business, medical) and hands-on experience in translating real-life documents.

name: Chinese Literary Heritage
description: Introduces pre-modern Chinese literature in translation. Topics chosen from classical poetry, short stories, novels, and drama. Emphasizes the interplay between orthodox values and the folk tradition. All readings are in English.

name: Pre-Modern Chinese Fiction in Translation
description: Pre-modern Chinese narrative from its philosophical and historical origins to the fiction at the turn of the 20th century. Emphasizes the 16th and 17th centuries when Chinese vernacular fiction flourished.

name: Modern Chinese Fiction in Translation
description: A survey of modern Chinese fiction in translation. Samples are from the early 20th century through the contemporary era and include writers of the early Republic, the P.R.C. and Taiwan. Focus is on fiction as a vehicle for social change. All readings in English. (H and N) (WR)

name: Tales of the Strange in Medieval Chinese Literature
description: Introduces traditional Chinese tales of the strange and primary sources that contributed to their development. Also covers cross-cultural literary theories of the fantastic and uncanny; interdisciplinary literary, discourse, and narrative theories; and three common medieval Chinese worldviews.

name: Writing Women in Chinese Literary Heritage
description: Investigates woman writers and the literary representation of women in classical Chinese literature. Readings include philosophical essays, poems, rhapsodies, biographies, narratives, moral lessons, and tales of the strange. Actively and critically applies modern academic theories and approaches to the study of literature.

name: Chinese Film and Media
description: Examination of Chinese cinema and other forms of media, such as television, music, and print culture in a broad sociopolitical and historical context. An interdisciplinary approach with a diversity of readings and multimedia tools incorporated into discussions.

name: Chinese Culture
description: Introduction to Chinese culture with emphasis on its philosophy, language, society, art, and people as a whole. All readings are in English.

name: All the Tea in China
description: Introduces the history, culture, and science of Chinese tea. Features primary literary and technical sources in translation, and secondary studies on tea as a beverage, a drug, a commodity, a currency, and a form of cultural capital. Analyze written, visual, and media sources using comparative perspectives and theories.

name: Chinese Martial Arts Fiction
description: Overview of Chinese martial arts fiction from earliest times to the present day. Discusses the literary pleasure of watching violence, the relationship between violence and the law, gender ambiguity of woman warriors, the imperial and (trans)national order of martial arts narrative, and the moral and physical economy of vengeance.

name: Taoism and Chinese Culture
description: Introduction to the general history and culture of Taoism in ancient and modern China: its thoughts, belief systems, cultural influences, practices, and rituals.

name: Bodies, Bodies, Bodies in Premodern China: Chinese Culture
description: Surveys a selection of classical approaches to the study of the body before analyzing and comparing several common literary, philosophical, medical (TCM), mantic, religious, and political representations of the human body in different eras of premodern Chinese culture. Tensions between traditionalism and modernity are examined in the final weeks of the course. All readings and discussion are in English.

name: Hong Kong, Taiwan, and the New Global Cinema: Hong Kong Taiwan Global Cinema
description: Overview of Sinophone film in Hong Kong, Taiwan, and the broader sphere of Chinese diaspora. Addresses film history, culture, and aesthetics.

name: Dream of the Red Chamber
description: Explores the intellectual and social life of traditional China through the 18th century epic novel, Story of the Stone. Also studies interpretive theories of the novel, both Chinese and Western. All readings are in English.

name: Journey to the West
description: Exploration of traditional Chinese religious culture, cultural history and literacy expression through a 100 chapter novel known as Journey to the West, or Monkey.

name: Classical Chinese 1
description: Introduction to classical Chinese prose with texts drawn mainly from early histories and philosophical writings (500 BC - AD 100). Emphasis on reading comprehension, grammar analysis and translation.

name: Readings in Chinese Literature
description: Introduces advanced language students to a sampling of Chinese writers. Materials chosen from classic or modern/contemporary Chinese literature rotated across semesters. All readings in Chinese. (H and N)

name: Penetration Testing: Ethical Hacking
description: Introduces principles and techniques associated with the cybersecurity practice known as penetration testing or ethical hacking. Covers planning, reconnaissance, scanning, exploitation, post-exploitation, and result reporting. Discover how system vulnerabilities can be exploited and learn to avoid such problems.

name: Enterprise Security
description: Provides an introduction to the real-world aspects of defending an enterprise network. Students will gain hands-on experience performing system security tasks and handling incidents. The class begins with a basic introduction to enterprise cybersecurity, the attack sequence, and managing cybersecurity. Then lecture, homework and lab activities cover the center for internet security's twenty essential security controls.

name: Information and Database Systems 1
description: First part of a two-course sequence that studies the essential concepts, principles and techniques of modern database systems. Topics include modeling and querying of data using conceptual data models as well as the development of a database application.

name: Computer and Information Security
description: Covers systematic threat and risk assessment; programmed threats and controls in hardware, software, and human procedures; security policies, models, and mechanisms; theoretical limitations and practical implementations; certification and accreditation standards; and case study reviews. Includes projects.

name: Introduction to Cryptology
description: Introduces classical and modern cryptography and cryptanalysis, including symmetric and asymmetric (public key) ciphers. Covers cryptographic hash functions, block and stream ciphers, as well as differential and linear cryptanalysis. Reviews applications of cryptography, cryptographic standards and protocols, and analyzes case studies of failed implementations.

name: CS Teaching & Learning
description: Covers basic pedagogy, especially as it relates to computer science and engineering, and covers three fundamental elements in education: learning environment, educational theory, and educational practice as approached to engineering-specific training.

name: Individual Study in CISE: INDIVIDUAL STUDY
description: Problems in different areas of computer science.

name: Senior Project
description: Involves completing a significant CISE-related project. Coordinate with the instructor and a project advisor, prepare a detailed technical report and deliver an oral presentation.

name: Special Topics in CISE: Reinforcement Learning
description: Variable content provides an opportunity for in-depth study of topics not offered elsewhere and of topics of current significance.

name: Practical Work
description: One term practical software engineering work under industrial supervision as set forth in the Herbert Wertheim College of Engineering regulations.

name: Co-Op Work in CISE
description: Practical engineering work under industrial supervision, as set forth in the Herbert Wertheim College of Engineering regulations.

name: Overseas Studies 1: Algorithm Design and Analysis
description: Provides a mechanism by which coursework taken as part of an approved study abroad program can be recorded on the UF transcript and counted toward graduation.

name: Penetration Testing -- Ethical Hacking
description: Introduction to the principles and techniques associated with the cybersecurity practice known as penetration testing or ethical hacking. The course covers planning, reconnaissance, scanning, exploitation, post-exploitation, and result reporting. The student discovers how system vulnerabilities can be exploited and learns to avoid such problems.

name: Computer and Information Security
description: Covers systematic threat and risk assessment; programmed threats and controls in hardware, software, and human procedures; security policies, models, and mechanisms; theoretical limitations and practical implementations; certification and accreditation standards; and case study reviews. Coursework includes a significant term project.

name: Introduction to Cryptology
description: Introducing classical and modern cryptography and cryptanalysis, including symmetric and asymmetric (public key) ciphers. It covers cryptographic hash functions, block and stream ciphers, as well as differential and linear cryptanalysis. It reviews BAN logic, applications of cryptography, cryptographic standards and protocols, and analyzes case studies of failed implementations.

name: Trustworthy Machine Learning
description: Explores research at the intersection of machine learning and security and privacy. Topics include: adversarial machine learning; differential privacy; membership inference; fairness & transparency; explainable/interpretable machine learning; deepfakes and disinformation.

name: Internet Data Streaming
description: Fundamental concepts, data structures and algorithms about extracting information from packet streams on the Internet in real time, with applications in network security, traffic engineering, e-commerce, and big data analytics

name: Individual Study
description: Individual Study

name: Supervised Research
description: Supervised Research

name: Special Topics in CIS: Internet Storage Systems
description: Special Topics in CIS

name: Graduate Seminar
description: Presentations by visiting researchers, faculty members, and graduate students.

name: Supervised Teaching
description: A supervised teaching experience.

name: Research for Master's Thesis
description: Research for Master's Thesis

name: Advanced Research
description: Research for doctoral students before admission to candidacy. Designed for students with a master's degree in the field of study or for students who have been accepted for a doctoral program. Not appropriate for students who have been admitted to candidacy.

name: Research for Doctoral Dissertation
description: Research for Doctoral Dissertation

name: Introduction to Corrections
description: Introduces the field of penology and corrections. Consideration is given to conflicting philosophies of punishment; criminological theory as it applies to the field of corrections; the selectivity of the process through which offenders move before their involvement in correctional programs; alternative correctional placements; and empirical assessments of the short-term and long-term consequences of involvement in correctional programs.

name: Careers in Criminal Justice
description: Advanced overview of professions available within the criminal justice system. Emphasis on the development of job seeking skills and strategies; local, state, federal and global employment opportunities; law and graduate school processes; building cultural competence and global perspectives.

name: Introduction to Law Enforcement
description: The role of the police in the criminal justice system of a democratic society. Topics include the organization of police work, discretion and the role of law enforcement in a socio-legal context.

name: Juvenile Justice
description: Examines the development, change and operation of the American juvenile justice system. Emphasizes the nature of juvenile law and the methods of dealing with youthful offenders.

name: Juvenile Justice
description: Introduces students to important topics related to the juvenile crime and juvenile justice. Discusses factors related to juvenile crime and societal responses to them. Discusses both classical and current research as well as policy and practice.

name: Law and the Legal Process
description: This survey course promotes an understanding of law as it relates to an individuals everyday encounters with the legal system. Actual legal cases may be studied to analyze how disputes are resolved by application of legal principles to factual situations, whether justice was served by the decision, and potential implications of the decision on future cases.

name: How Does US Law Affect Wildlife?
description: Course on US-based wildlife and environmental law. Pressing legal issues concerning fish and wildlife conservation law and policies. Crosses biological, ecological, criminological, historical, and legal issues.

name: Law and Society
description: Introduces the scholarly study of law from a multidisciplinary, liberal arts perspective. Examines legal ideas, legal institutions and the legal process with an emphasis on the study of criminal behavior and the American criminal justice process.

name: Psychology and Law
description: Application of behavioral science research and practice to the legal system. Topics include psychologists and the legal system; lawyers' socialization, training and ethics; legality, morality and justice; forensic assessment; the insanity defense; competence in the legal system; eyewitness identification; jury selection; theories of crime; and punishment and sentencing.

name: Juvenile Law
description: Examines the juvenile justice system, including delinquency, dependency and laws that apply especially to juveniles. Studies operation of the Florida juvenile code and the relationship between children and society.

name: Criminal Law
description: Studies substantive criminal law, including historical development, the tension between social and legal definitions of crime, the basic dimensions of criminality, the specific elements of major crimes and the nature of criminal sanctions.

name: Criminal Procedure
description: Studies constitutional rights of the accused in criminal proceedings. Focuses on analysis of case materials involving the law of arrest, search and seizure, the use of confessions, fair trial and the prohibition of cruel and unusual punishments.

name: Law and Society
description: Interdisciplinary examination of relationship between legal and social orders. Focuses on various functions of law, different forms of legal thought, development of law, and the impact of law/sanctions on society.

name: Law and Social Science
description: The interface between law and knowledge from various social scientific disciplines, including psychology, sociology, history, and anthropology.

name: Democracy in Theory and Action
description: The birth and evolution of democracy and its contributions to western civilization and current forms of government and governing. Lively dialogue between ancient democracy and modern through a comparative analysis, tackling some of the most pressing issues, such as limits of political participation and free speech, the role of the press/media, and elitism in politics.

name: Gardens to Read and Visit
description: Investigation of gardens as cultural artifacts in literature and art to discover the extent to which gardens are sites of comfort as well as contest, through analysis of the tension between the experience (“to visit”) and the representations (“to read”) of gardens in written and visual forms.

name: Medicine, Science, and the Dawn of Reason
description: This interdisciplinary course invites students to examine the passage of humanity into the era of reason and the development of medical science and ethics. As part of the “nature and culture” theme, it presents a historical narrative on the passage of humanity from superstition to the era of scientific inquiry as represented throughout the Western canon and world literatures.

name: The Glory That Was Greece
description: Exploration of the historical, cultural, and socio-political aspects of the Ancient Greek world as it is situated firmly within the western classical tradition.

name: The Grandeur That Was Rome
description: Provides a multi-faceted introduction to the culture of Rome and its contribution to western civilization and canon. Primary source material read in translation.

name: Classical Antiquity and Sustainability
description: Examines classical antiquity, applying methods and theories of sustainability to explore the impact of the ancient Greeks and Romans on their environment and focusing on the distribution of wealth, social stratification, land use and classical representations of the natural world.

name: Athens in Topography and Monuments
description: Explores the topography and monuments of ancient Athens to understand social, historical, economic and religious institutions.

name: Greece Today and Yesterday
description: Interdisciplinary examination of various aspects of ancient and modern Greek life and culture.

name: Pompeii: An Archaeological Laboratory
description: Studies the material remains of a Roman town through an examination of the excavated finds: architecture, wall-paintings, and inscriptions.

name: Ancient Egypt
description: Studies the civilization, culture, and monuments of ancient Egypt from prehistoric times to the New Kingdom and Late period.

name: The Athenian Democracy
description: Studies ancient Athens from c.650-322 BCE, with attention to the political, social, and cultural institutions of the democracy, drawing on primary sources and modern theory to explain democratic changes from the archaic to the classical period.

name: Classical Greece
description: Studies the social, political, and cultural developments of classical Greece from the Persian Wars to the death of Alexander (500-322 BCE).

name: Sport and Recreation in the Ancient World
description: Examines literary and archaeological sources to determine the social, economic, political and cultural importance of games in the ancient Mediterranean world from the time of Homer to the fall of the Roman Empire.

name: Gender and Sexuality in Classical Antiquity
description: Explores perceptions of the masculine and feminine in Ancient Greece and Rome, discussing these stereotypes in their political, social, economic, and cultural contexts.

name: Classical Archaeology
description: Illustrated lectures on archaeology, its process of discovery, and methods. History of major archaeological exploration in Mediterranean lands compared with extant literary information.

name: The Ancient City: Roman Cities
description: Studies the cities of the Roman Empire from the founding of Rome to the establishment of Constantinople as the Eastern capital. Emphasizes life in imperial Rome and in European and North African cities.

name: AI in Antiquity and Today
description: Examines AI’s origins in ancient Greece and compares it to AI’s acceptance and use in modern society. Pairs discussion of Greek and Roman philosophical and other literary texts on the soul and identity and the boundaries between the natural and artificial with emerging societal issues related to AI, including gender, racism, and slavery.

name: Crime and Punishment in Ancient Athens
description: Examines how the Athenians defined, regulated, and suppressed crime and what the political discourse on crime reveals about Classical Athens.

name: Experiential Learning in Classical and Ancient Studies
description: Offers credit for experiential learning engagement and reflection related to the discipline of classical and ancient studies.

name: Special Topics in Classical Civilization: Multilingualism
description: Examines various aspects of Greek and Roman culture based on the ancient sources, literary, and archaeological.

name: Individual Study
description: Reading, conference and reports. All work in will be in translation.

name: Undergraduate Research in Classical Civilization
description: Provides firsthand, supervised research in Classical Civilization. Projects may involve inquiry, design, investigation, scholarship, discovery or application in Classical Civilization.

name: Classics Capstone Seminar: CLASSICS CAPSTONE
description: Introduces scholarly literature on a significant topic in classics. Students will write a research paper showing proper use of primary and secondary sources on the topic.

name: Overseas Studies 1: Greek Art&Architecture
description: Provides a mechanism by which coursework taken as part of an approved study abroad program can be recorded on the UF transcript and counted toward graduation.

name: Augustan Age
description: In-depth investigation of history, political organization, literature, and society of Augustan Rome.

name: Greek and Roman Archeology
description: Grounding in monuments of ancient Greece and Roman, and history and methodology of classical archeology.

name: The Classical Research Tradition
description: Research methods in the classics.

name: Athenian Law and Society
description: Comprehensive assessment of structures of classical Athens, offering detailed study of Athenian law, constitution, society, gender relations, and culture. Ancient life linked with modern debate on similar issues.

name: Individual Work
description: Readings and reports in Classical civilization.

name: Greece and the Near East
description: Rotating topics concerning political, economic, diplomatic, and cultural interaction between Greek world and its neighbors in the East.

name: Topics in Classical Civilization
description: Intensive study of a particular topic in ancient classical civilization which is not offered every academic year and is not covered by existing course numbers/titles. Past topics have included Ancient Sculpture Methods, Slavery in Antiquity, Women in Ancient Greece and Rome, Roman Religion, etc. The reading material for this course will generally consist of secondary literature and ancient literature in translation. Students will produce a final research paper or project in the topic.

name: Personal Growth
description: Introduces the concepts and techniques in psychology that apply to personal growth and development. All students have the opportunity to participate in research projects or alternative experiences.

name: Abnormal Psychology
description: The varieties of disordered experience and conduct, and their contribution to an understanding of more effective personal and social adjustment. Includes the neuroses, psychoses and psychosomatic and conduct disturbances.

name: Introduction to Clinical Research
description: Hands-on, faculty-supervised research experience in an area of interest. Introduces current research techniques, including the design and development of clinical research projects and data analysis. Three hours of laboratory work or other research activity (e.g., literature searches, grant preparation, recruitment of study participants, etc.) are required for each credit.

name: Eating Disorders
description: Overview of the causes and treatments associated with the full range of recognized eating disorders, including anorexia, bulimia and binge eating disorder, as well as a variety of subclinical forms of problematic eating behaviors and their surrounding factors and issues.

name: Introduction to Clinical Child/Pediatric Psychology
description: Survey and exploration of the science and practice of clinical child/pediatric psychology, including application of clinical science to problems faced by children and their families. Course also emphasizes assessment and intervention methodologies related to child behavior and health.

name: Introduction to Clinical Psychology
description: Survey and exploration of contemporary roles of clinical psychologists. Also emphasizes the integration of science and practice when solving problems of individuals, families, and groups.

name: Introduction to Health Psychology
description: Survey and exploration of the science and practice of clinical health psychology. Also emphasizes application of the biopsychosocial model of health and illness to health promotion, disease prevention, and the treatment and rehabilitation of existing illness and disability.

name: Introduction to Neuropsychology
description: Survey and exploration of the science and practice of clinical neuropsychology. Emphasizes discussion of major neuropsychological disorders and the mechanisms underlying higher cognitive function.

name: Clinical and Behavioral Neuroanatomy and Lab
description: Provides lecture and laboratory study of the human central nervous system and behaviors. Gain knowledge for engaging in basic clinical problem solving by laying a foundation of neurophysiological and neuroanatomical principles.

name: Diagnosis and Treatment Planning
description: Introduces categories of diagnosis and their application in psychotherapy and treatment planning. Analyzes diagnosis processes and diagnostic categories in sociocultural context.

name: Human Higher Cortical Functioning
description: Models that explain linkages between brain and behavior. Focus on both functions and dysfunctions.

name: Psychological Treatment I
description: Current dynamic and personality theories, practices, and related research in psychotherapy.

name: Clinical Psychological Assessment
description: Introduction to concepts, theory, and practices in clinical psychological assessment across the lifespan.

name: Lifespan Psychopathology
description: Diagnostic issues, theoretical formulas, clinical manifestations, and research related to child and adult psychopathology across the lifespan.

name: Measurement, Research Design, and Statistical Analysis in Clinical Psychology I
description: Integration and interaction among research design, tests and measurements, and statistics.

name: Measurement, Research Design, and Statistical Analysis in Clinical Psychology II
description: Continuation of CLP 6527C.

name: Applied Multivariate Methods in Psychology
description: Application of multivariate methods (MANOVA, discriminant functions, factor analysis, SEM) to research problems in psychology.

name: Graduate Foundations of Professional Ethics in Clinical Psychology
description: Guides clinical psychology grad students through ethical and professional dilemmas, including research conduct. Reviews APA’s Ethical Principles and Code of Conduct. Covers ethical decision-making models to support competent, ethical practice across clinical, research, teaching, and management roles.

name: Individual Work
description: Reading or research in areas in clinical psychology.

name: Supervised Research
description: Supervised Research

name: Supervised Teaching
description: Supervised Teaching

name: Core Practicum in Clinical Psychology
description: Supervised training in appropriate work settings.

name: Advanced Practicum in Neuropsychology
description: Supervised clinical experience in neuropsychological assessment and cognitive rehabilitation of patients with neurologic impairments.

name: Advanced Practicum in Applied Medical Psychology
description: Supervised clinical experience in inpatient and outpatient consultation, assessment and intervention with psychosomatic, stress-related, and somatopsychic disorders.

name: Practicum in Intervention
description: Designed for individual with special interests and needs.

name: Advanced Practicum in Clinical Psychology
description: Advanced trainees practice application of evidence-based clinical skills in assessment, intervention, and consultation, and further skills in the appropriate use of clinical supervision and patient advocacy. Students will be assigned placement with an Advanced Practicum rotation and supervisor by the Director of Clinical Training and Area Head(s). The trainee and individual supervisor will establish individual and/or group supervision times, location, and preferred methods of communication.

name: Research for Master's Thesis
description: Research for Master's Thesis

name: Child and Family Treatment in Clinical Psychology
description: Introduces students to evidence-based practice in the area of child and family therapy for a variety of childhood psychological disorders and family difficulties. This course will review concepts of assessment, case conceptualization, treatment planning, measurement of treatment outcomes, intersectionality, and ethics.

name: Advanced Health Psychology and Behavior Medicine
description: Theory, research, and clinical applications related to core topic areas. Special attention to pathophysiology, research methods, issues of diversity, and ethical concerns.

name: Advanced Psychotherapy in the Practice of Clinical and Health Psychology
description: Intended for third, fourth-, and fifth-year graduate students in Clinical and Health Psychology who wish to advance their intervention competencies with adult patients with complex comorbid mental/behavioral disorders and physical health conditions. The course is appropriate for students who have met expectations on all core assessment competencies and have begun to develop advanced intervention competencies.

name: Cognitive and Clinical Approaches to Functional Neuroanatomy
description: The purpose of this course is to provide the student with lecture and laboratory study of the human central nervous system. Emphasis is put on the relationship between structure and function in the central nervous system with focus on higher cortical function and anatomy. A key goal of this course is to provide students with introductory knowledge for engaging in basic clinical problem solving.

name: Neuropsychological Lifespan Assessment
description: Research, theory, and basic procedures.

name: Best Methods for Studying Psychological Change
description: Application of change methods (ongiudinal mixed effects, latent growth models, survival analysis) to research problems in psychology.

name: Cognitive and Affective Bases of Behavior
description: Advanced seminar for in-depth examination of selected issues and topics.

name: Special Topics In Clinical Psychology: Clinical Psychological Assessm
description: Advanced seminar for in-depth examination of selected issues and topics.

name: Internship
description: Reading assignments and conferences. Must include 1500 work hours; designed as a 2-semester sequence.

name: Advanced Research
description: Research for doctoral students before admission to candidacy. Designed for students with a master's degree in the field of study or for students who have been accepted for a doctoral program. Not appropriate for students who have been admitted to candidacy.

name: Research for Doctoral Dissertation
description: Research for Doctoral Dissertation

name: Classical Mythology
description: Examines selection of myths, or sacred stories, of the Ancient Greeks and Romans, and the numerous ways they used these stories, including through history, literature, philosophy, art and architecture. Explores how aspects of Greek and Roman civilization have contributed to Western culture. Analyzes major works of the Western canon based on these myths and their adaptations.

name: Survey of Roman Literature
description: Critical study of the development of Roman literature. Includes readings from Plautus, Cicero, Catullus, Vergil, Ovid, and Tacitus. Read in translation.

name: Greek Drama
description: Classical Greek theater: archaeological remains of important theaters and selected plays of Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides, Aristophanes, and Menander. Read in translation.

name: Myths of the Greeks and Romans
description: Development, importance, and influence of Graeco-Roman mythology. The main Greek and Latin literary sources are read in translation.

name: Religions of the Graeco-Roman World
description: Development, importance, and influence of Greek and Roman religion and cult practice. The main literary and epigraphical sources are read in translation.

name: Ancient World in Film
description: Examines film and television characterizations of the ancient world and how these accord with known facts through historical and archaeological evidence. Viewing of selected movies along with background readings, lectures, and discussion.

name: Special Topics in Classical Literature: Conspiracy Theory Anc/Modern
description: Examines various aspects of Greek and Roman literature with focus on special genres (e.g., historiography), periods (e.g., the age of Augustus), or subjects (e.g., slavery).

name: Individual Study
description: Reading, conference and reports. All works are read in translation.

name: Computer Network Fundamentals
description: Fundamental concepts, principles, and standards of computer networks. Introduces topics in top-down approach, starting with the application layer in the OSI system architecture with a stronger focus on application, transport, and network layers.

name: Multimedia Networking Principles
description: Design and analysis of multimedia networking. Major effort is devoted on multimedia elements, and their impact on higher-level protocols at the application- and transport-layer.

name: Computer Networks
description: Design, implementation, and internals of networks. Routing, congestion control, internetworking, TCP/IP, optimization, and proxy services.

name: Computer and Network Security
description: Issues, analysis, and solutions. Viruses, worms, logic bombs, network attacks, covert channels, steganography, cryptology, authentication, digital signatures, electronic commerce.

name: Mobile Computing
description: Emerging topics of wireless and mobile computing and networking including mobile computing models, mobile-IP, adhoc networks, Bluetooth, and 802.11b. Mobile database access and mobile transactions in context of emerging field of M-commerce.

name: Advanced Computer Networks
description: Computer network architecture, including topologies, media, switching, routing, congestion control, protocols, and case studies.

name: Distributed Multimedia Systems
description: Design issues; survey of recent advances, including compression, networking, and operating system issues.

name: Introduction to Communication Studies
description: Introduces various theoretical perspectives for understanding human communication. This course affords students an understanding of the basic social and behavioral science concepts and principles used in the analysis of behavior and past and present social, political, and economic issues.

name: Collaboration With AI for Better Communication
description: Two pivotal questions in the realm of modern communication: “How can we communicate effectively in a world with AI?” and “How can AI tools be utilized for effective communication and collaboration for better social decisions?” Explore both the positive potential and the challenges posed by AI in professional/science communication, fostering a balanced and critical understanding of these tools. Emphasizes its interdisciplinary nature to explore the impact of AI on social institutions, structures, and processes, highlighting the intersection between technology and social science. Engage with key themes, principles, and methodologies used in social and behavioral sciences, applying them to understand and navigate the AI-influenced communication landscape.

name: Siri is My Superpower: Communicating with AI
description: Explores AI by describing how we communicate with others in the world and the tools we use to do so. Examines how we communicate with AI by introducing what a communicator, a mediator, and intelligence are.

name: Organizational Communication
description: Explores the processes, practices, and difficulties of communication among large groups engaged principally in the work environment. Examines organizational structures, patterns of communication, task and social roles, extrinsic influences, and methods of producing intrinsic motivation and innovation.

name: Organizational Communication
description: Explores the processes, practices, and difficulties of communication among large groups engaged principally in the work environment. Examines organizational structures, patterns of communication, task and social roles, extrinsic influences, and methods of producing intrinsic motivation and innovation.

name: Global and Cultural Issues in Health Communication
description: Explores the complex associations among communication and the many contexts, issues, and relationships surrounding health and well-being in the world. Investigates cultural, historical, social, and ethical meanings of health and illness. Considers issues in global health, culture, and communication in health care initiatives.

name: Interpersonal Conflict Management
description: Introduces fundamental communication skills, principles, theories and research relevant to effective conflict management in a variety of interpersonal contexts and relationships.

name: Family Communication
description: Provides students with an understanding of how communication functions to develop, maintain, enrich, or limit family relationships.

name: Health Communication
description: Surveys theory, research and practice of communication in the contexts of healthcare and health promotion. (WR)

name: Beyond the Human: AI, Hybrid Minds, and the Changing Nature of Communication
description: As artificial intelligence reshapes how we think, create, and communicate, this course asks a foundational question: What does it mean to be human in an age of intelligent machines? This seminar approaches AI not as a technical tool, but as a philosophical and social artifact—a mirror through which humanity examines its own cognition, ethics, and meaning making. We draw from communication theory, social psychology, and philosophy of technology to explore how intelligent systems challenge assumptions about identity, agency, authorship, and social structure. Alongside foundational frameworks such as Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) and sociological theories of meaning (Symbolic Interactionism, Structuration Theory), the course integrates emerging perspectives including Social Approval Theory of Technology Adoption (SATAT) and Machine–Human Reflexivity (MCP/MHP/MSP). These approaches move beyond HCI’s individual level and situate AI within broader social and institutional contexts. Students will examine AI as both an object and subject of communication, using personal experiences to reflect on the emergence of hybrid minds and moral responsibility in algorithmic environments. Through readings, discussion, and writing, the course encourages ethical inquiry, theoretical depth, and self-reflexive insight.

name: Language & Social Interaction
description: Explores the role of language in social interaction, covering theories and methods investigating language in social interaction, ways language is used to construct social identity, and issues concerning language and culture. Classroom activities and homework involve how (non)verbal conduct is enacted and understood in social situations.

name: Language and Power
description: Explores the role of language in articulating, maintaining, and subverting power relations in society. Drawing from Communication Studies and Applied Linguistics, the course provides the tools to uncover, describe, and critically analyze the various strategic biases in language that create and reinforce power asymmetries in society.

name: Undergraduate Research in Communication Studies: UG RES COMM STUDIES
description: Provides firsthand, supervised research in Communication Studies. Projects may involve inquiry, design, investigation, scholarship, discovery or application in Communication Studies.

name: Special Topics in Communication: Storytelling
description: Seminar study of theory and research in a specific area of communication.

name: Grant Writing
description: The course provides students with an opportunity to develop grant writing and project development skills. Students will learn how to work collaboratively to conceptualize a grant proposal and develop standard proposal components, including project goal, background, logic model, approach, and budget. Students will also work individually to conduct preliminary research.

name: Risk Communication
description: Examine theory and research related to the communication of health, environmental, technological, agricultural, and geological risks. Explore risk communication from multiple perspectives, including psychological, social, and cultural. Emphasis on understanding, critiquing, and applying theories of risk communication.

name: Computer Programming for Engineers: COMP PRG ENGR MATLAB
description: Computer programming and the use of computers to solve engineering and mathematical problems. Emphasizes applying problem solving skills; directed toward technical careers in fields employing a reasonably high degree of mathematics. The programming language used depends on the demands of the departments in the college. Several languages may be taught each semester, no more than one per section. Those required to learn a specific language must enroll in the correct section.

name: Computer Programming for Engineers Laboratory: COM PRG ENG MATLAB LAB
description: Optional laboratory for COP 2271. Required for ISE majors.

name: Python Programming for Engineers
description: Introduction for those who have little experience in programming and have been looking to obtain hands-on learning experience in the Python programming language. Encourages developing problem solving and computational thinking skills in an engineering field and emphasizes a reasonably high degree of mathematics.

name: C++ Programming for Engineers
description: Introductory course for those who have little experience in programming and have been looking to obtain a hands-on learning experience to the C++ programming language. Developing problem solving and computational thinking skills in an engineering field is encouraged in this course and emphasized with a reasonably high degree of mathematics.

name: Computer Programming Using JAVA
description: In-depth treatment of computer programming using JAVA. Problems related to a variety of disciplines are solved. Introduces the basic concepts of software and hardware; develop a variety of stand-alone applications and applets. For non-CISE majors only.

name: Programming Fundamentals 1
description: First course of a two-semester introductory sequence for those planning further study in computer science, digital arts and sciences or computer engineering. Concepts of computer science and the process of computer programming, including object-oriented programming, procedural and data abstraction and program modularity.

name: Programming Fundamentals 2
description: Second course of a two-semester introductory sequence for those planning further study in computer science, digital arts and sciences or computer engineering. Concepts of computer science and the process of computer programming, including object-oriented programming, procedural and data abstraction and program modularity.

name: Advanced Programming Fundamentals for CIS Majors
description: Fast-paced introduction to computer science for those with prior programming experience. Explores major concepts of computer science and the process of computer programming, including object-oriented programming, procedural and data abstraction and program modularity.

name: Data Structures and Algorithm
description: Algorithm development using pseudo languages, basic program structures, program design techniques, storage and manipulation of basic data structures like arrays, stacks, queues, sorting and searching and string processing. Linked linear lists. Trees and multilinked structures.

name: Programming Language Concepts
description: Introduces programming language principles, including language constructs, design goals, run-time structures, implementation techniques and exposure to a wide variety of programming paradigms.

name: Object-oriented Programming
description: Fundamental conceptual models for programming languages illustrated with specific programming languages and application problems. Specific topics include class and object models, inheritance among classes, objects and static and dynamic systems and implementations.

name: Algorithm Abstraction and Design
description: Covers algorithmic concepts and their use rooted in practical application and computer science theory. Topics include algorithmic paradigms, limits of computing, and algorithm time complexity classes.

name: Operating Systems
description: Design and implementation of various components of a modern operating system, including I/O programming, interrupt handling, process and resource management, computer networks and distributed systems.

name: Information and Database Systems 2
description: Part two of a two-course sequence. Provides a basic understanding of the internals of a modern database system. Topics include data storage, indexing, query processing and advanced concepts such as database tuning, alternate data models and emerging applications. (M)

name: Advanced Data Structures
description: Development of efficient data structures used to obtain more efficient solutions to classical problems, such as those based on graph theoretical models, as well as problems that arise in application areas of contemporary interest.

name: Programming Language Principles
description: History of programming languages, formal models for specifying languages, design goals, run-time structures, and implementation techniques, along with survey of principal programming language paradigms.

name: Distributed Operating System Principles
description: Concepts and techniques for efficient management of computer system resources.

name: Database Management Systems
description: Introduction to systems and procedures for managing large computerized databases.

name: Database System Implementation
description: DBMS architecture, query processing and optimization, transaction processing, index structures, parallel query processing, object-oriented and object-relational databases, and related topics.

name: Applications of Discrete Structures
description: Covers the mathematics of discrete events; i.e., events that involve distinct elements, finite structures of distinct elements or finite sampled versions of continuous phenomena (such as movement).

name: Computational Methods for Chemical Engineers
description: Solutions of scientific and engineering problems using digital computers. Formulation of models for describing physical processes, numerical analysis, and computer programming.

name: Numerical Analysis: a Computational Approach
description: Numerical integration, nonlinear equations, linear and nonlinear systems of equations, differential equations and interpolation.

name: Analysis of Algorithms
description: Introduction and illustration of basic techniques for designing efficient algorithms and analyzing algorithm complexity.

name: Computational Geometry
description: Design, analysis, and implementation of algorithms and date structures to solve geometric problems. Applications in graphics, robotics, computational biology, data mining, and scientific computing. Convex hulls, Voronoi diagrams, triangulations, arrangements, and range searching.

name: Mathematics for Intelligent Systems
description: Mathematical methods commonly used to develop algorithms for computer systems that exhibit intelligent behavior.

name: Formal Languages and Computation Theory
description: Introduction to theoretical computer science including formal languages, automata theory, Turing machines, and computability.

name: Comparative Politics Introduction
description: Classification of political systems according to institutional and developmental characteristics. Causes and costs of political stability and instability. Comparison will relate to contemporary political institutions and processes in specific countries.

name: Culture and Politics
description: Addresses interactions among culture and politics through analysis of concepts including perspective, world view, ethos, cultural norms, etc. Themes may include: identity politics; Other as subject vs. object; religion; cultural expectations regarding political institutions; and dynamics both within and across local and/or national communities.

name: Democracy in Dark Times
description: Democratic decline across several counties and regions of the world. Addresses periods of democratic decline in regions in which democracy is expected, as well as in countries with histories of authoritarianism. Themes include Nazism, fascism, socialist and/or populist revolution, as well as democratic recovery in some cases.

name: Western European Politics
description: Comparative analysis of the government and politics of the major Western European countries. Emphasizes party systems and the social bases of politics in industrialized societies.

name: African Politics
description: African nationalism, political movements and governments in the African states.

name: Introduction to Latin American Politics
description: Introductory overview of political patterns and political behavior in Latin America within comparative and developmental perspectives. Emphasizes the social, economic, and political factors shaping contemporary political structures and processes.

name: Topics in Israeli Politics and Society
description: Addresses Israeli politics and society from a Comparative Politics or an International Relations perspective, depending upon instructor. May address Israeli politics at the grassroots, elite, societal, domestic, international, or micro-levels. Themes may include social movements, institutional configuration, religious-secular dynamics, immigration, ethnic politics, gender, foreign relations, international organizations, or other issues.

name: Eastern European Politics
description: Comparative analysis of the formal structures of government and politics of Eastern European countries; the actual operation of their political systems and the factors that influenced their transitions to democracy and market-based economies.

name: Politics in Russia
description: Analyzes the formal structures of government and politics in Russia, the actual operation of its political system and the factors that influenced the transition to democracy and a market-based economy.

name: Comparative Law and Courts
description: Addresses the politics of law and courts in comparative perspective in regions and country cases around the world. Regions and country cases vary with instructor. May include themes such as: judicial power and politics, judicial independence, rights revolutions, legal mobilization, legal profession, legal culture, and/or constitutional development in comparative perspective.

name: Women and Politics in the Modern Middle East
description: Examines women and gender in the politics of the modern Middle East from the late 19th century through the 1990s.

name: Selected Studies in Comparative Politics: Euro Politics&Society
description: Variable topics in comparative politics; precise course content will be announced in advance.

name: Politics in Developing Nations
description: Introduces politics in third world states, an examination of common problems and the various strategies for dealing with them.

name: Politics under Authoritarianism
description: Investigates the sources of durable authoritarianism in Asia and around the world and contrasts the survival of dictatorships with successful democratic transitions.

name: Comparative Elections
description: Comparative Elections

name: Social Movements and Contentious Politics in Europe
description: Provides tools to analyze why, when, and how social movements engage in collective action and protest in a variety of European contexts. Appropriate for advanced students in the social sciences and the European track in IDS International Studies.

name: Irish Government and Politics
description: Intensive analysis of the contemporary history, politics and government of Ireland. The course examines the foundations of the state and society from an historical and political-cultural perspective.

name: Argentina and the Politics of Memory
description: Politics of Argentina from the 19th century to the present with special focus on Peronism and the rise of democracy.

name: The Politics of Ethnic Conflict
description: Introduces the systematic study of communal violence, to the major concepts in conflict studies, to the main approaches to studying conflict and to many of the major episodes of communal violence in contemporary Asia and beyond.

name: Judaism and Politics
description: Examines how Jews govern themselves (often referred to as communal governance) and how Jews relate to the political system where they live. Explores the development of the Jewish political tradition in the Biblical period, the Middle Ages, the early modern period and the modern era.

name: Democratization in Global Perspective
description: Introduces literature on democratization, including familiarization with important theoretical and conceptual issues and empirical data on major regions of the world.

name: Undergraduate Research in Comparative Politics: UG RES COMP POLITICS
description: Provides firsthand, supervised research in Comparative Politics. Projects may involve inquiry, design, investigation, scholarship, discovery or application in Comparative Politics.

name: Advanced Topics in Comparative Politics
description: Advanced Topics in Comparative Politics

name: Social Movements in Comparative Perspective
description: Examines major classical and contemporary theoretical approaches to the field of collective action and social movements.

name: Introduction to Comparative Political Analysis
description: Introduction to major theoretical and methodological approach to study of comparative politics.

name: Comparative Qualitative and Mixed Methods
description: Critically analyzes comparative and mixed methods from concept formation, qualitative measurement, dimensionality, single, comparative, longitudinal-historical and mixed case study approaches from the perspective of multiple causal ontologies and causal assesment.

name: West European Politics
description: Western European politics with emphasis on Britain, France, Spain, and Scandinavia. Addresses major themes in the politics of these nation-states or sub-regions. Addresses key relevant theories.

name: Seminar in African Politics
description: Study of African politics in comparative perspective.

name: Latin American Politics I
description: Latin American Politics I

name: Modern Middle East Politics
description: An historical institutionalist approach to the development of the modern Middle East in the move from empire to nation-state, addressing several important themes in 20th and 21st century Middle East politics. Readings include top-down as well as bottom-up analyses.

name: Ethnicity and Nationalism
description: Introducing the main approaches to the study of how ethnic and national identities are formed, and how they are activated in politics. Exploration of various forms of ethnic politics: peace, rioting, and the most extreme forms, genocide and secession.

name: Democratization and Regime Transition
description: Review of structural, institutional, and cultural dimensions of democratization, with special attention to Latin America, Africa, and Eastern Europe.

name: Post-Communist politics
description: Analysis of problems associated with democratic transition and market reform in the post-communist countries of Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union.

name: Comparative Elections and Party Systems
description: Major issues related to the study of elections and political parties in the comparative context. Specifically, we will discuss the relationship between political parties and electoral institutions in authoritarian, democratic, and transitioning political systems.

name: The European Union In Comparative Perspective
description: Graduate level introduction to the study of the European Union from a comparative perspective. Assuming familiarity with graduate level comparative politics (CPO 6091), but no previous knowledge of the EU is required. The EU is analyzed as a comparative case through an institutionalist perspective.

name: Beginning Fiction Writing
description: For students who want to write fiction. Includes basics and heavy reading. Students write stories and their fiction is discussed in workshop.

name: Beginning Poetry Writing
description: Concentrates on basics of reading and writing poetry. Some student writing will be discussed in workshop.

name: Fiction Writing
description: Instruction in basic techniques of voice, plot and character while introducing advanced ones.

name: Poetry Writing
description: Writing poetry may become an addiction. This workshop continues with matter-of-fact techniques and some fancy ones as well. Students write poems and read some difficult and thrilling poetry of the past and present. By the end, students may be able to say, with Humpty Dumpty, I can explain all the poems that ever were invented - and a good many that haven't been invented just yet. Juniors or seniors who have not taken CRW 1101 or CRW 1301 must have strong composition skills. (C) (WR)

name: Advanced Seminar in Fiction Writing
description: Small workshop for students who have made their way out of beginner's workshops with sanity intact. Now the work gets more difficult, more deranged and more delightful. Emerson said, "People do not deserve to have good writing, they are so pleased with bad." Admission by manuscript review during advanced registration (refer to department website); by prerequisite during drop/add.

name: Advanced Seminar in Poetry Writing
description: "More reeling and writhing," as Lewis Carroll said. An intense workshop for a small group of poets who have stared at the Pacific with a wild surmise. Like Balboa - or was it Cortez? Admission by manuscript review during advanced registration (refer to department website); by prerequisite during drop/add.

name: Creative Nonfiction
description: Creative writing workshop which introduces genres of creative nonfiction (e.g. memoir, personal essay, travel writing) and provides training in those genres. Appropriate for, but not limited to, English majors.

name: Senior Advanced Workshop in Fiction Writing
description: For students who want to trouble the literary editors and readers of the future. Many members of this class have gone on to graduate school in writing. Ants eat everything that is written, said an explorer. This is a workshop for ants. Admission by manuscript review during advanced registration (refer to department website); by prerequisite during drop/add.

name: Senior Advanced Workshop in Poetry Writing: Back in the Ozone Again
description: George I said, "I hate all Boets and Bainters." For battle-scarred veterans of previous workshops who now want the full treatment, this is a small workshop for serious poets who want to write their names in water, as long as they are also in the Norton Anthology. Students often go from this class into MFA programs in poetry. Admission by manuscript review during advanced registration (refer to department website); by prerequisite during drop/add.

name: Fiction Writing
description: Fiction Writing

name: Studies in Literary Form: Forms of Fiction
description: Formal aspects of literature.

name: Verse Writing
description: Verse Writing

name: Individual Work
description: Individual study in reading literature and criticism, required for MFA specialization in creative writing.

name: Hydrodynamics
description: Classification and properties of fluids, hydrostatics, and conservation of mass, momentum and energy in fluid flow. Potential flow, similitude and physical modeling. Laminar and turbulent pipe flow. Introduces turbomachines.

name: Hydraulics
description: Fundamental equations for pipe and open conduit flow. Development of design oriented formulas for pipes and open channels. Introduces hydrology.

name: Urban Stormwater Systems Design
description: Surface-water system design including: time of concentration, peak runoff rate, open-channel flow, gravity storm sewer, culvert, stormwater pumping, filtration systems, hydrograph generation, flood routing, site layout, site grading and permitting.

name: Water Resources Engineering
description: Study of water resources engineering applications including hydrology and statistics, groundwater, hydraulic machinery, dams and reservoirs, water quality, water quality modeling, water and waste-water treatment and water law and institutions.

name: Groundwater Flow I
description: Porous media flow. Darcy's law. Conservation of mass. Laplace equation. Flownets. Well hydraulics.

name: Advanced Surface  Hydrology
description: Physical and quantitative concepts and principles of hydrologic processes and their engineering applications. Reynolds Transport Theorem, the Continuity and Momentum Equations applied to phenomena and processes. Hydrologic analyses, including unit hydrograph theory, lumped flow routing, and distributed flow routing. Engineering concepts of hydrologic design, design storms and hydrologic chemistry.

name: Mixing and Transport in Turbulent Flow
description: Applying fluid mechanics to problems of turbulent mixing and transport of substances in the natural environment.

name: Environmental Biochemistry of Trace Metals
description: Environmental impact and fate of trace metals and metalloids as they cycle through geological and biological environmental compartments. Emphasizes anthropogenic activities of metals with growing environmental concerns, including arsenic, mercury, chromium, and lead.

name: Advanced Urban Stormwater Systems Design
description: Stormwater system design including: time of concentration, peak runoff rate, open-channel flow, gravity storm sewer, culvert, stormwater pumping, filtration systems, hydrograph generation, flood routing, site layout, site grading and permitting.

name: Contaminant Subsurface Hydrology
description: Physical-chemical-biological concepts and modeling of retention and transport of water and solutes in unsaturated and saturated media. Applications of environmental aspects of soil and groundwater contamination.

name: Introduction to Czech Language and Culture 1
description: CZE 1130 and its sequel, CZE 1131, offer a comprehensive introduction to Czech, using interactive methods to develop competence in speaking, listening, reading, writing and cultural interaction.

name: Introduction to Czech Language and Culture 2
description: Continuation of series. A comprehensive introduction to Czech, using interactive methods to develop competence in speaking, listening, reading, writing and cultural interaction.

name: Intermediate Czech 1
description: Builds reading and writing skills while continuing to develop conversational ability and listening comprehension. Using a communicative approach, provides an overview of Czech grammar.

name: Intermediate Czech 2
description: Continuation of intermediate study. Goal is to further develop speaking, listening, reading and writing skills.

name: Fundamentals of Dance Technique
description: Practice and principles of fundamentals and stylistic characteristics common to ballet, jazz and modern dance, including styles from the Western canon.

name: Contemporary Dance Practices 1: BA/BFA
description: Experience in beginning level technique, readings, observations and movement exploration.

name: Contemporary Dance Practices 2: BA/BFA
description: Experience in contemporary approaches to dance technique, readings, observations and movement exploration.

name: Contemporary Ballet Practices 1: Non-majors/Minors
description: Basic ballet technique with discussion of terminology and history.

name: Contemporary Ballet Practices 2: BA/BFA
description: Contemporary perspectives in basic ballet technique with discussion of terminology and history.

name: West African Dance and Music
description: Introduces traditional West African dance and music. Focuses on the learning of material emphasizing practice and performance with application to classroom and outreach-oriented projects.

name: Contemporary African & African Diasporic Dance Practices 1: Afro-Brazilian (Dance Majors)
description: Develops understanding of various styles of dance within the African and African Diasporic realms as a movement practice and an art form; performance based.

name: Contemporary African & African Diasporic Dance Practices 2: Hip-Hop
description: A performance-based course aimed at developing the understanding of various styles of dance within the African & African Diasporic realms as a movement practice and an art form.

name: World Dance and Intercultural Performance
description: Introduces the performance of traditional and popular dance styles representing a selection of world dance perspectives. Emphasizing practice and performance, the course examines dance forms in relation to their specific cultural contexts. Readings, video viewing and class projects enhance laboratory exploration. (H and N)

name: Tap 1
description: Beginning-level tap course which covers fundamental rhythms, sounds, techniques, vocabulary, and provides a foundational knowledge of tap history. Although geared toward students pursuing a career in musical theatre, all interested in tap are welcome.

name: Broadway Dance Styles 1
description: By focusing on the mid-20th century through approximately the year 2000, learn original Broadway and other musical theatre choreography that continue to shape the landscape of dance today, as well as develop the rigorous work ethic necessary for a career in the professional entertainment industry.

name: Broadway Styles 2
description: Learn original Broadway and other musical theatre choreography by focusing on material from approximately the year 2000 through the present, and help develop the rigorous work ethic necessary for a career in the professional entertainment industry.

name: Dance Composition 1: Majors
description: Introduces improvisation and composition with emphasis on process and movement elements. Solo choreography.

name: Dance Composition 2
description: Practice and study of basic compositional crafting, emphasizing solo and small group works.

name: Dance Improvisation
description: Introduces dance improvisation as an art form, a personal practice, and a process for creating choreography through movement exploration, readings, and observations.

name: First Year Dance Ensemble
description: Develops technical range and performance skills through the study and production of dance repertory.

name: Cohort Dance Ensemble
description: Develops technical range and performance skills through the study and production of dance repertory.

name: Somatics 1: BFA
description: Rotating topics feature physical disciplines that support bodily awareness and athletic conditioning.

name: Somatics 2
description: Rotating topics feature physical disciplines that supports bodily awareness and athletic conditioning.

name: Friday Movement Practice
description: Friday Movement Practice is a weekly meeting in which Dance majors gather to dance together, led by a rotating roster of faculty and guest artists. It is one way in which the School of Theatre + Dance seeks to engage students in the experience of a broad range of movement methods and approaches, and to provide opportunities for all students to dance in community. Additionally, an important part of professional development is interacting with working artists in the field.

name: Contemporary Dance Practices 3
description: Experience in intermediate level technique, readings, observations and movement exploration exercises.

name: Contemporary Ballet Practices 3
description: Intermediate ballet technique with discussion of terminology and theory.

name: Pointe
description: Instruction in pointe technique with the study of variations from classical ballet repertory.

name: Contemporary African & African Diasporic Dance Practices 3: Hip Hop
description: A performance-based course aimed at developing the understanding of various styles of dance within the African & African Diasporic realms as a movement practice and an art form.

name: Tap 2
description: For those who already have an established tap foundation and explores faster and more complex tap material. Although geared toward students pursuing a career in musical theatre, all interested in tap are welcome.

name: Dance Composition 3
description: Practice and study in choreography with focus on various compositional styles, both traditional and nontraditional.

name: Dance Composition 4
description: Practice and study in choreography of group works, including theory and aesthetics.

name: Contemporary Dance Practices 4: BFA
description: Advanced level techniques, readings, observation, informal performance and movement exploration exercises.

name: Modern Dance 4-2
description: Offered in Miami only.

name: Contemporary Ballet Practices 4: BFA
description: Advanced ballet technique with discussion of terminology and style.

name: Contemporary African & African Diasporic Dance Practices 4: Afro-Fusion
description: Develops the understanding of various styles of dance within the African and African Diasporic realms as a movement practice and an art form; performance based.

name: Dance Ensemble
description: Experience in dance ensemble: preparation, performance and production.

name: Summer Dance Intensive
description: An intensive workshop including technique (ballet, jazz, modern, multicultural), improvisation, composition, repertory, production work and culminating in performance.

name: Special Topics in Dance: Advanced Somatics for Dancers
description: Lecture, seminar or studio sessions covering selected topics of current interest in dance.

name: Dance Teaching Methods
description: Methods and skills for teaching in ballet, modern and jazz, including theory and practice.

name: Dance Teaching Methods 2
description: Continues dance teaching methods. Each student will prepare and teach a 90-minute ballet class. The course also incorporates lecture, class discussion, videos and active participation to provide the fundamental skills necessary to teach classical ballet.

name: Dance, Race, Gender
description: From ballet to Beyoncé, explores how dance and social identities, such as race and gender, impact each other. Explore social, concert, and popular dance in the US and select global contexts in a seminar-style course with occasional movement workshops. No dance experience is required.

name: Is There Culture in Dance and Music
description: Students will explore music and dance as living culture in Lagos and Bahia by examining their cultural, social, and political significance. Through dance, media, and language studies, students reflect on their own cultural experiences and develop empathy and self-awareness by understanding shared humanities.

name: Body, Self, World: Movement through Lived Experience
description: This course offers students the opportunity to transform thoughts into movement expression. Students will engage in movement-based experiences through a series of labs. Weekly discussions allow for discoveries about the mind-body connection through readings about phenomenology and somatic practices, including how these are applied to styles and concepts from the Western canon.

name: Dance Appreciation
description: This course surveys the development of dance as an art form within human culture. The course focuses on seminal dance works, including the Western canon, while cultivating an understanding of dance's historical, artistic, and cultural significance.
